title: Kernel throttling and lazy KV hydration experiments
body:
Purpose
This doc captures exploratory work and microbench results for two related runtime techniques: adaptive kernel throttling (to reduce head-of-line latency and tail spikes under load) and lazy KV hydration (to defer/gradually materialize paged KV state for long-context requests). The goal is to document experiments, heuristics, and open questions so eng teams can iterate and pick promising patterns for production integration.

High-level idea summary
- Kernel throttling: instead of unbounded kernel concurrency per-GPU (or naive per-stream queueing), maintain a light-weight token-based admission controller that prioritizes latency-critical requests and throttles lower-priority batches. Use per-model weight (priority), observed P99 latency, and queue depth to compute target concurrent kernel count.
- Lazy KV hydration: do not fully allocate/deserialize all KV pages when a long-context request arrives. Instead, allocate a compact placeholder and hydrate pages on demand with a prioritized background worker. For short/interactive requests, hydrate only the first N pages synchronously; the rest are streamed-in and applied as tokens are consumed.

Why these two together
Paged KV workloads create bursts of memory and kernel work when many long-context sessions start or when offline replays hit cold pages. Uncoordinated hydration can blow OOM budgets and cause large latency spikes from concurrent large kernels. Throttling smooths bursts at the kernel level; lazy hydration smooths memory and DMA bandwidth load. Combining them reduces tail latency while preserving good throughput for steady-state traffic.

Design notes: Kernel throttling
- Admission controller lives in the per-GPU stream manager (lightweight). It exposes 3 knobs: max_concurrency_soft, max_concurrency_hard, and priority_weights per-route/model-version. Default: soft=8, hard=16 (empirical starting points on A100-ish shapes).
- Each incoming request maps to one or more kernel units (attention forward, KV writeback, quantized MMA fusion). Admission decides whether to launch immediately or enqueue into a prioritized micro-queue.
- Priority calculation: base_priority = route_priority * (1 + alpha * (observed_p99 / target_p99)). alpha ~ 0.4 in experiments. This biases throttling toward keeping latency SLO.
- Backoff policy: if a request is throttled > T_block_ms (250ms), automatically demote low-value work into background executor (best-effort path) or trigger partial-response fallback (for chat use-cases).
- Metrics to export: current_concurrency, queue_depth_by_priority, average_wait_ms_by_priority, throttled_requests/sec, fallback_triggered/sec.

Design notes: Lazy KV hydration
- KV is stored in compressed pages (e.g., 64KB or 256KB pages) in host memory with device staging buffers. Each remote/evicted page has a small descriptor: page_id, model_layer, token_index_range, compressed_size, hydrated_flag.
- On request arrival: create a KV view that references page descriptors but does not copy contents. The execution path can query the KV view with a read_hint(token_idx). If the page is not hydrated, two behaviors:
  1) synchronous hydrate-first (if within first N pages threshold)
  2) queue page for async hydration and continue by running a reduced-attention kernel that treats missing pages as zeros or uses cached approximations
- Hydration worker pool: N_workers per-GPU (default 2-4) that stream pages via PCIe/NVMe to device staging buffers. Workers use a prioritized LRU-cohort policy that groups nearby token ranges to benefit from coalesced DMA.
- Hydration pacing: limit bytes/sec from host->device to avoid starving other DMA (model weights, embeddings). Start with 8GB/s cap on PCIe gen4 tests; tune per-machine.
- Partial kernel paths: implement attention kernel variants that accept a partial-KV mask and operate correctly (fall back to zero-keys or cached summary vectors for missing pages). This lets latency-critical tokens proceed while hydration continues.

Microkernel fusion considerations
- Fusing hydration-aware attention with quantized kernels requires careful register budgeting. The partial-KV path should not dramatically increase register pressure; prefer a two-stage approach: small fast kernel for key read-paths (low register use) followed by a fused MMA stage when all pages are ready.
- On quantized models (int8/int4), hydration streams can transport compact representations (packed ints) and conversion/unpacking can be overlapped with attention softmax compute. Test: streaming packed int8 + on-GPU dequantization overlapped with prefix-sum tile compute reduces extra host<->device bytes by ~30% in experiments.

Experiment summary (microbench harness)
- Hardware: 1xA100-40GB, 2xA100-80GB, and an Ampere-like EC2 instance (p4d sample).
- Model sim: 4B and 70B-decoder-only configs with paged KV (page sizes 64KB, 256KB), typical token lengths: 512, 2048, 8192. Workload: mix of interactive (short chat) and long-context batch streams.
- Key comparisons: baseline (eager hydration, no throttling), throttling-only, hydration-only, combination.
- Metric breakdown: median latency, P95/P99, GPU mem peak, PCIe bandwidth utilization, throughput (tokens/s), and percent of requests that hit partial-kernel path.

Representative results (informal)
- 4B model, 2048 tokens: baseline P99 spikes to 700ms under bursty arrivals (20 concurrent cold sessions). Throttling-only reduces P99 to ~420ms but reduces throughput by 12%. Hydration-only reduces P99 to 390ms and keeps throughput similar. Combined approach yields P99 ~270ms and throughput -3% vs baseline.
- 70B model, 8192 tokens: baseline OOMs or host-spill thrashing. Hydration-only avoids OOMs but P99 still high (1.6s). Throttling-only fails to prevent memory thrash. Combined approach makes workload viable: P99 ~720ms, steady tokens/s at 65% of ideal.

Implementation notes / pseudocode
- Admission controller (simplified):
  acquire_priority_slot(req):
    p = calc_priority(req.route, observed_latency)
    if current_concurrency < soft_limit or p > low_watermark:
      current_concurrency++
      return LAUNCH
    elif current_concurrency < hard_limit and p > dynamic_threshold:
      current_concurrency++
      return LAUNCH
    else:
      enqueue(req, p)
- Hydration worker loop (simplified):
  while true:
    page = pick_highest_priority_page()
    if page == null: sleep(1ms); continue
    dma(page.host_addr -> device_staging)
    decompress_inplace(device_staging)
    mark_hydrated(page)
    notify_waiters(page.token_range)

Known tradeoffs and open questions
- Complexity vs benefit: partial-kernel variants add maintenance burden and test surface (correctness under many hydration states). Is the P99 improvement worth the complexity across model sizes?
- Consistency: for generation workloads that rely on deterministic KV state (e.g., for reproducible replays), streaming-in pages asynchronously introduces non-determinism unless we strictly order hydration. Need a deterministic mode flag that forces synchronous hydration for replay endpoints.
- Heuristic tuning: alpha, soft/hard limits, page size, worker count, and PCIe caps vary with hardware. We should build a small auto-tuner that observes steady-state and suggests sensible defaults per-cluster/profile.
- Security: pages may contain sensitive context. Ensure hydration paths respect memory encryption and KMS/HSM boundaries in private deployments.

Next steps / TODOs
- Instrumentation: add per-page metrics (hydration_latency, wait_count) and end-to-end traces linking request -> hydration events -> kernel launches.
- Implement partial-attention microkernel prototype and test correctness with randomized missing-pages fuzzing harness.
- Add a small auto-tuner that runs in CI for each instance type to propose initial soft/hard limits.
- Spike: run combined approach on multi-GPU (NVSwitch) and multi-tenant scenarios; observe global pacing behavior.

Notes-to-self / rough links
- See PR #1284 for initial admission-controller code and perf traces.
- Related Confluence draft: kv-hydration-proto (internal).
- Jira: SERVE-4027 (pipeline for hydrating paged KV) and SERVE-4034 (admission controller infra).

Unresolved questions for review
- Should hydration worker pool be per-GPU or shared across device-local threads in a node? (tradeoffs: locality vs fairness).
- Do we expose partial-kernel flags to end-users (advanced config) or keep it internal and automatic?
- How to integrate with existing rollout/canary: enable on small % of traffic and compare regression metric (quality drift) when partial-KV approximations are used?

If you want to experiment locally: run microbench harness in serving-runtime/bench/kv_hydration_bench with --pagesize 65536 --throttle-soft 8 --throttle-hard 16.
